claims.text: High lattice distortion in refractory high-entropy alloys creates local strain fields.
Local strain fields caused by lattice distortion impede dislocation mobility.
High lattice distortion stabilizes the thermoelastic response of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Partially substituting a refractory element with an element having a more similar atomic size will reduce the spread in atomic radii and overall lattice distortion.
The proposed partial elemental substitution can reduce lattice distortion while retaining high-entropy character.
Variation in constituent atomic sizes governs the level of lattice distortion.
Reducing atomic-size variance diminishes local strain fields.
Diminished local strain fields reduce dislocation pinning and increase dislocation mobility.
Reduced dislocation pinning caused by lower lattice distortion will lower high-temperature mechanical strength.
The lower-distortion alloy will have lower high-temperature yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The lower-distortion alloy may have a higher high-temperature creep rate than the baseline alloy.
The lower-distortion alloy will have a modified thermal expansion coefficient and less thermoelastic stability than the baseline alloy.
The baseline high-distortion alloy has superior mechanical and thermoelastic behavior at high temperatures.
Grain-boundary effects, solid-solution strengthening, and other competing mechanisms may affect the magnitude of the predicted property changes.
The comparison is intended to hold grain size, phase distribution, loading, temperature, and environmental conditions constant between baseline and modified alloys.
A lack of statistically distinguishable degradation in strength or thermoelastic behavior, or a lack of increased dislocation mobility, would falsify the proposed lattice-distortion mechanism.
